Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

issues.explanation: The trigger set suggests a highly specific external threat context involving cyclists and thrown objects, but the rest of the profile (memory and appraisals) does not contain corresponding content about that kind of event. In a man-made disaster profile, 'burnt smell' coheres with disaster-related sensory memory, whereas 'people cycling' and 'throwing objects' pull toward a different trauma scenario and are hard to integrate with the remaining items.

'Avoid seeing friends' is not well supported by the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation strongly links Triggers with Memory and Maladaptive Strategies, and the endorsed strategies are otherwise cognitive/internal (thought avoidance, thought monitoring). Social avoidance could occur in PTSD, but here it is not tied to any endorsed trigger, memory content, or appraisal pattern, making it look like a strategy for a different symptom cluster than the one described.

vignette:
Martin is a 55-year-old single man of European descent who works as a counselor at a community mental health center. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 74, seeking help for the first time following a man-made disaster that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. Martin was present at a warehouse fire caused by an industrial accident in his neighborhood - a fire that spread rapidly and with terrifying speed, trapping several people inside. He was among the bystanders who attempted to help, pulling a woman through a broken window while the structure groaned and smoke poured in thick, acrid waves around them. The smell of burning material - synthetic, chemical, nothing like a campfire - saturated his clothes and hair for days afterward. At one point, a panicked man nearby hurled a fire extinguisher across the pavement in desperation, the clatter of metal on concrete cutting through the roar of the flames. Martin made it out. Not everyone did.

In the weeks that followed, Martin noticed that the smell of smoke - from a neighbor's fireplace, from a passing vehicle's exhaust, from anything that carried even a faint char - would stop him cold. The burnt smell in particular, so specific to that afternoon, seemed to reach inside him and pull something loose. These olfactory triggers did not merely remind him of the event; they transported him into the emotional core of it, flooding him with fear and helplessness before he had time to register what was happening. Similarly, the sound or sight of objects being thrown - even a colleague setting down a heavy binder with a thud - could produce the same sudden activation. As these triggers began to surface memory, Martin found himself caught in fragmentary, disorienting recall: not clear images, but the smell of that smoke arising unbidden during the memory itself, and waves of raw emotional intensity that arrived without any accompanying picture, as though the terror had been encoded separately from everything else. Perhaps most unsettling to him was the quality of the memory itself - it felt, he told his intake clinician, like something that had happened to a stranger, like footage from someone else's life that he had somehow absorbed. He could not make it feel like his own.

Martin had come to believe, with quiet but firm conviction, that his body had turned against him - that its continued alarm responses were evidence of something broken and unreliable. He was certain that he had to stay vigilant at all times, because the disaster had proven to him that catastrophe could arrive without warning. These appraisals did not sit passively alongside his memory; they actively colored it, lending every recollection a quality of ongoing threat, as though the danger had never truly ended. And in turn, the memory reinforced these beliefs - each intrusive wave of emotion without image seemed to confirm that he was not processing things normally, that something was fundamentally wrong with him.

To manage this, Martin had developed a set of strategies that made intuitive sense to him but were quietly narrowing his life. He had stopped seeing friends, partly because social gatherings sometimes involved fireplaces or candles, and partly because he feared losing control of his reactions in front of others. He had made a determined effort to avoid thinking about the event at all, believing - with some force - that if he allowed himself to dwell on it, he would not be able to cope, that he would unravel entirely. But suppressing thought about the event had an ironic consequence: the memories became more intrusive, more fragmentary, and more emotionally raw, as though the material that had never been processed kept pressing back against the door he had shut. He had also begun monitoring his own thoughts with exhausting vigilance, scanning for any sign that he was losing his grip on sanity. This constant internal surveillance left him little cognitive room for anything else.

At work, the strain had become impossible to ignore. Martin counsels clients who have experienced trauma, and the work now costs him enormously - a client describing a fire in a session, or the faint smell of smoke drifting in from outside the building's ventilation system, could destabilize him for the rest of the afternoon. He had begun scheduling fewer clients and leaving early on difficult days, and his supervisor had noticed. It was this - the fear that his professional life, the one domain that had always anchored him, was slipping - that finally brought Martin to seek help. What he is most afraid of is that the damage is permanent. What he most hopes is that he can feel, once again, like the events of that day belong to him - and that he might be able to bear them.
